claim: The invariant cleavage pattern of ascidian embryos is characterized by three rounds of UCDs in two vegetal-posterior blastomeres from the 8-cell stage onwards, leading to the formation of two small germline precursor cells at the 64-cell stage.
source: The invariant cleavage pattern of ascidian embryos is characterized by three rounds of UCDs in two vegetal-posterior blastomeres from the 8-cell stage onwards, leading to the formation of two small germline precursor cells at the 64-cell stage (Figure 1A; Hibino et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1A showing embryo development stages and citation to Hibino et al., 1998

claim: The CAB attracts the mitotic spindle and is consistently inherited in the smallest blastomeres that will give rise to the germline precursors.
source: These UCDs are due to spindle attraction by the CAB (Nishikata et al., 1999; Prodon et al., 2010), which is consistently inherited in the smallest blastomeres that will give rise to the germline precursors.
evidence: Supported by citations to Nishikata et al., 1999 and Prodon et al., 2010

claim: The orientation of the third cleavage is thought to be determined by the CAB attracting one mitotic spindle pole thereby conferring the slanted shape of the 8-cell stage embryo.
source: Before these three canonical UCDs, the orientation of the third cleavage is thought to be determined by the CAB attracting one mitotic spindle pole thereby conferring the slanted shape of the 8-cell stage embryo with the CAB located in the pair of vegetal-posterior blastomeres B4.1 (Figure 1B; Negishi et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1B and citation to Negishi et al., 2007

claim: The vegetal blastomeres at the 8-cell stage, containing the CAB, are larger than their animal siblings.
source: However, the vegetal blastomeres at the 8-cell stage, containing the CAB, are larger than their animal siblings (Nishida, 2005; Sardet et al., 2007), raising the question why the CAB is inherited by the larger, rather than the smaller daughter cell as found in subsequent UCDs.
evidence: Supported by citations to Nishida, 2005 and Sardet et al., 2007

claim: Vegetal blastomeres are larger than their animal siblings at the 8-cell stage in P. mammillata embryos.
source: To address this question, we first confirmed the size asymmetry between the animal and the vegetal blastomeres in P. mammillata embryos by measuring cell volumes from 3D reconstructed live 8-cell stage embryos and found that vegetal blastomeres are indeed larger their animal siblings (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by 3D reconstruction measurements shown in Figure 1C

claim: The size asymmetry is slightly but significantly more pronounced in the anterior compared to the posterior pairs of blastomeres at the 8-cell stage.
source: Our measurement also showed that the size asymmetry is slightly but significantly more pronounced in the anterior compared to the posterior pairs of blastomeres (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 1C with statistical significance indicated

claim: At metaphase, the spindle in the posterior blastomere B3 is not parallel to the animal-vegetal axis of the embryo but is slightly tilted by 9.6°.
source: Sagittal views (Figure 2A) showed that, at metaphase, the spindle in the posterior blastomere B3 is not parallel to the animal-vegetal (AV) axis of the embryo but is slightly tilted by 9.6° as observed previously (Negishi et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by measurements from sagittal views in Figure 2A and citation to Negishi et al., 2007

claim: Spindle tilting becomes more pronounced at anaphase onset with an angle of 21.3° due to the rapid displacement of the vegetal spindle pole toward the CAB.
source: This tilting became more pronounced at anaphase onset with an angle of 21.3° due to the rapid displacement of the vegetal spindle pole toward the CAB (Figure 2A, B), suggesting that the CAB attracts the spindle.
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 2A and 2B

claim: The spindle was centered along its axis at metaphase and then became vegetally off-centered at anaphase onset in posterior blastomeres.
source: Consistent with such a role of the CAB at anaphase onset, the spindle was centered along its axis at metaphase and then became vegetally off-centered at anaphase onset (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 2C

claim: The larger size of the vegetal daughter blastomeres (inheriting the CAB) is set at anaphase onset in posterior blastomeres.
source: Interestingly, however, cleavage plane prediction on 2D confocal sections showed that the larger size of the vegetal daughter blastomeres (inheriting the CAB) is set at anaphase onset (Figure 2D), even though the spindles were attracted toward the CAB (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: Supported by cleavage plane predictions shown in Figure 2D

claim: A mechanism other than spindle off-centering generates the UCD in the posterior blastomere B3 pair.
source: This suggests that a mechanism other than spindle off-centering generates the UCD in the posterior blastomere B3 pair.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that larger vegetal cells form despite spindle attraction toward CAB

claim: No clear spindle displacement was observed during the division of the anterior blastomere A3 pair in sagittal views.
source: Contrary to the posterior blastomere B3 pair, no clear spindle displacement was observed during the division of the anterior blastomere A3 pair in sagittal views (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: Supported by observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C

claim: Imaging anterior A3 blastomeres in transversal views revealed the presence of a spindle tilting by 5.67° occurring at anaphase onset apparent by a lateral displacement of the vegetal spindle pole away from the vegetal pole.
source: Imaging anterior A3 blastomeres in transversal views revealed the presence of a spindle tilting by 5.67° occurring at anaphase onset apparent by a lateral displacement of the vegetal spindle pole away from the vegetal pole (VP; Figure 2E, F).
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 2E and 2F

claim: The spindle was slightly off-centered toward the animal pole in anterior blastomeres at anaphase onset.
source: In addition, the spindle was slightly off-centered toward the animal pole in anterior blastomeres at anaphase onset (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 2G

claim: The larger size of the vegetal daughter blastomere is set at anaphase onset in anterior blastomeres, coinciding with the timing of both spindle off-centering and tilting.
source: Cleavage plane prediction on 2D confocal sections showed that the larger size of the vegetal daughter blastomere is set at anaphase onset (Figure 2H), coinciding with the timing of both spindle off-centering and tilting.
evidence: Supported by cleavage plane predictions shown in Figure 2H

claim: Spindle tilting at anaphase onset is a common feature in both anterior A3 and posterior B3 blastomeres, preceding UCD.
source: Collectively, these findings reveal that spindle tilting at anaphase onset is a common feature in both anterior A3 and posterior B3 blastomeres, preceding UCD.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of spindle tilting in both anterior and posterior blastomeres

claim: UCD occurred only when tilting is applied to the spindle in virtual simulations using real cell contours.
source: For both cases, we measured the predicted cleavage plane and found that UCD occurred only when tilting is applied to the spindle (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by virtual simulation results shown in Figure 3A

claim: Spindle tilting can contribute to UCD independently of spindle off-centering.
source: This supports the notion that spindle tilting can contribute to UCD independently of spindle off-centering.
evidence: Inferred from virtual simulation results showing UCD with centered but tilted spindles

claim: When a virtual spindle was gradually tilted in an anisotropic geometry (half-circle), UCD occurred as the cleavage plane was gradually shifted from the center of mass.
source: However, when we gradually applied a tilting of the virtual spindle, UCD occurred in the anisotropic geometry as the cleavage plane was gradually shifted from the cente of mass, whereas no UCD occurred in the isotropic geometry as the cleavage plane always crossed the center of mass (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by virtual simulation results shown in Figure 3B

claim: No UCD occurred in the isotropic geometry (circle) when spindle tilting was applied as the cleavage plane always crossed the center of mass.
source: However, when we gradually applied a tilting of the virtual spindle, UCD occurred in the anisotropic geometry as the cleavage plane was gradually shifted from the cente of mass, whereas no UCD occurred in the isotropic geometry as the cleavage plane always crossed the center of mass (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by virtual simulation results shown in Figure 3B

claim: Anisotropy of cell shape can lead to off-centering of the cleavage plane, an effect associated to the activity of spindle tilting in UCD.
source: This suggests that anisotropy of cell shape can lead to off-centering of the cleavage plane, an effect associated to the activity of spindle tilting in UCD.
evidence: Inferred from virtual simulation results comparing isotropic and anisotropic geometries

claim: Membrane-labeled embryos at 4-cell stage treated with low concentration of Cytochalasin B displayed distinct and localized membrane invaginations at the animal pole of both anterior A3 and posterior B3 blastomeres at anaphase onset.
source: Membrane-labeled embryos at 4-cell stage treated from Nuclear Envelop Breakdown with low concentration of Cytochalasin B to weaken the actomyosin cell cortex, displayed largely normal embryo shape, but also showed distinct and localized membrane invaginations at the animal pole of both anterior A3 and posterior B3 blastomeres at anaphase onset (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by observations shown in Figure 4A

claim: Membrane invaginations in Cytochalasin B-treated embryos were dependent on microtubules since they were completely abolished when embryos were treated with Nocodazole to depolymerize microtubules.
source: Membrane invaginations in Cytochalasin B-treated embryos were dependent on microtubules since they were completely abolished when embryos were treated with Nocodazole to depolymerize microtubules (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: No membrane invaginations were detected at the VP in Cytochalasin B-treated embryos.
source: Furthermore, while no membrane invaginations were detected at the VP, some invaginations were observed at the CAB site (visible by a dense membrane staining) in posterior B3 blastomeres and at the anterior/lateral side in anterior A3 blastomeres (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by observations shown in Figure 4A

claim: Some membrane invaginations were observed at the CAB site in posterior B3 blastomeres and at the anterior/lateral side in anterior A3 blastomeres.
source: Furthermore, while no membrane invaginations were detected at the VP, some invaginations were observed at the CAB site (visible by a dense membrane staining) in posterior B3 blastomeres and at the anterior/lateral side in anterior A3 blastomeres (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by observations shown in Figure 4A

claim: The VP of both anterior A3 and posterior B3 blastomeres is devoid of microtubule cortical pulling forces even though the spindle was pointing toward this domain.
source: These findings are consistent with the previously reported ability of the CAB to effectively pull on the spindle at 4-cell stage (Negishi et al., 2007), but also indicate that the VP of both anterior A3 and posterior B3 blastomeres is devoid of microtubule cortical pulling forces even though the spindle was pointing toward this domain.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of membrane invaginations at the VP despite spindle orientation toward it, with citation to Negishi et al., 2007

claim: The observed cortical pulling forces are sufficient to explain the spindle tilting motion observed in those blastomeres, suggesting that no other mechanism may be involved.
source: Importantly, the observed cortical pulling forces are sufficient to explain the spindle tilting motion observed in those blastomeres, suggesting that no other mechanism may be involved.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of membrane invaginations matching the spindle tilting behavior

claim: Staining of yolk granules showed a homogeneous distribution in oocytes and no AV gradient at the 4-cell stage, with yolk evenly accumulating at the cell periphery.
source: However, staining of yolk granules showed a homogeneous distribution in oocytes and no such AV gradient at the 4-cell stage, with yolk evenly accumulating at the cell periphery (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by yolk staining observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B

claim: Astral microtubules in live embryos were able to reach the vegetal cortex of these cells at anaphase onset.
source: Consistent with this, we found that astral microtubules in live embryos, which become detectable in mitosis from anaphase onset, were able to reach the vegetal cortex of these cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by live imaging observations shown in Figure 4B

claim: The lack of microtubule pulling forces at the VP is not due to microtubules being unable to reach the cortex, but rather that this cortex is devoid of microtubule pulling force generators.
source: We thus conclude that the lack of microtubule pulling forces at the VP, as evidenced by the lack of membrane invagination in Cytochalasin B-treated embryos, is not due to microtubules being unable to reach the cortex, but rather that this cortex is devoid of microtubule pulling force generators.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that microtubules reach the VP but no membrane invaginations occur there

claim: In VP-ablated embryos, membrane invaginations were present at both poles of the embryo.
source: Consistent with our assumption of the VP not exerting pulling forces, we found that in VP-ablated embryos, membrane invaginations were present at both poles of the embryo (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by observations in VP-ablated embryos shown in Figure 4C

claim: VP-ablated embryos had an equal division in the anterior lineages and an inverted UCD in the posterior lineages at the third cleavage.
source: Such VP-ablated embryos had an equal division in the anterior lineages and an inverted UCD in the posterior lineages at the third cleavage (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by cell volume measurements shown in Figure 4D

claim: Proper UCDs leading to larger vegetal blastomeres were maintained after control ablation of the animal pole or the posterior pole (containing the CAB).
source: In contrast, proper UCDs leading to larger vegetal blastomeres were maintained after control ablation of the animal pole or the posterior pole (containing the CAB) (Figure 4D; note that gastrulation occurred normally in those control ablation, Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by cell volume measurements shown in Figure 4D and gastrulation observations in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C

claim: The VP contains a polarity domain necessary for proper spindle tilting and, consequently, the generation of larger vegetal blastomeres.
source: These microsurgery experiments suggest that the VP contains a polarity domain necessary for proper spindle tilting and, consequently, the generation of larger vegetal blastomeres.
evidence: Inferred from the results of VP ablation experiments showing altered cell division patterns

claim: The anisotropic shape of mitotic blastomeres at the 4-cell stage is characterized by large cell–cell contacts and a pronounced long axis of the cell oriented along the AV axis of the embryo.
source: The anisotropic shape of mitotic blastomeres at the 4-cell stage is characterized by large cell–cell contacts and a pronounced long axis of the cell oriented along the AV axis of the embryo (Figure 2A, E).
evidence: Supported by observations shown in Figure 2A and 2E

claim: Blastomeres at the 4-cell stage do not undergo mitotic rounding when transiting from interphase to mitosis, apparent by cell sphericity decreasing rather than increasing.
source: This elongated cell shape is due to these cells not undergoing mitotic rounding when transiting from interphase to mitosis, apparent by cell sphericity decreasing rather than increasing, as expected for cells undergoing mitotic rounding (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by cell sphericity measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: An increase in mother cell sphericity was associated with a decrease of the UCDs in the anterior lineages and an inversion of the size asymmetry in the posterior lineages.
source: Consistent with our expectations, 3D cell reconstructions before and after the division showed that an increase in mother cell sphericity was associated with a decrease of the UCDs in the anterior lineages and an inversion of the size asymmetry in the posterior lineages (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-E).
evidence: Supported by 3D reconstruction measurements shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-E

claim: Spindle tilting and spindle off-centering still occurred between metaphase and anaphase in isolated anterior A3 and posterior B3 blastomeres, suggesting that the activity of the polarity domains is maintained in such isotropic cell shape.
source: Live observation of the mitotic spindle in isolated anterior A3 and posterior B3 blastomeres further showed that spindle tilting and spindle off-centering still occurred between metaphase and anaphase, suggesting that the activity of the polarity domains is maintained in such isotropic cell shape (Figure 5C-H).
evidence: Supported by live imaging observations shown in Figure 5C-H

claim: Contrary to the situation in anisotropic blastomeres, the spindle tilting is incapable of inducing UCD in isotropic blastomeres, and, consequently, spindle off-centering led to a strongly reduced UCD in anterior A3 blastomeres and an inversion of UCD in posterior B3 blastomeres.
source: Yet, contrary to the situation in anisotropic blastomeres, the spindle tilting is incapable of inducing UCD in these isotropic blastomeres, and, consequently, spindle off-centering led to a strongly reduced UCD in anterior A3 blastomeres and an inversion of UCD in posterior B3 blastomeres (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 5B

claim: AV compression led to spindle alignment in the plane of the compression (perpendicular to the AV axis) and its displacement in direction to the posteriorly located CAB in posterior B3 blastomeres.
source: As expected, AV compression led to spindle alignment in the plane of the compression (perpendicular to the AV axis) and its displacement in direction to the posteriorly located CAB in posterior B3 blastomeres and, consequently, an inversion of the directionality of the UCD in the posterior B3 blastomeres with the CAB now being inherited in the smaller daughter cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by observations in compressed embryos shown in Figure 6B

claim: AV compression resulted in an inversion of the directionality of the UCD in the posterior B3 blastomeres with the CAB now being inherited in the smaller daughter cells.
source: As expected, AV compression led to spindle alignment in the plane of the compression (perpendicular to the AV axis) and its displacement in direction to the posteriorly located CAB in posterior B3 blastomeres and, consequently, an inversion of the directionality of the UCD in the posterior B3 blastomeres with the CAB now being inherited in the smaller daughter cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by observations in compressed embryos shown in Figure 6B

claim: The combined activities of cell geometry and polarity domains determine spindle off-centering and UCD.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that the combined activities of cell geometry and polarity domains determine spindle off-centering and UCD.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of blastomere isolation and compression experiments

claim: Cell division orientation is thought to result from a competition between cell geometry and polarity domains controlling the position of the mitotic spindle during mitosis.
source: Cell division orientation is thought to result from a competition between cell geometry and polarity domains controlling the position of the mitotic spindle during mitosis.
evidence: Represents established scientific understanding in the field

claim: Cell geometry and polarity domains cooperate, rather than compete, in positioning the cleavage plane during UCDs in early ascidian embryos.
source: Here, we show that cell geometry and polarity domains cooperate, rather than compete, in positioning the cleavage plane during UCDs in early ascidian embryos.
evidence: Main conclusion of the study based on experimental data

claim: The UCDs and their orientation at the ascidian third cleavage rely on the spindle tilting in an anisotropic cell shape, and cortical polarity domains exerting different effects on spindle astral microtubules.
source: We found that the UCDs and their orientation at the ascidian third cleavage rely on the spindle tilting in an anisotropic cell shape, and cortical polarity domains exerting different effects on spindle astral microtubules.
evidence: Main finding of the study based on experimental data

claim: The spindle position during UCD is set by the combined activities of cell geometry and polarity domains, where cell geometry modulates the effect of cortical polarity domain(s).
source: We therefore propose that the spindle position during UCD is set by the combined activities of cell geometry and polarity domains, where cell geometry modulates the effect of cortical polarity domain(s).
evidence: Main conclusion of the study based on experimental data

claim: A yet unknown polarity domain localized in the vegetal cortex, devoid of cortical microtubule pulling forces, is necessary for UCD of anterior cells.
source: We also identified a yet unknown polarity domain localized in the vegetal cortex, devoid of cortical microtubule pulling forces, which is necessary for UCD of anterior cells.
evidence: Main finding of the study based on experimental data

claim: The century old observation of cells dividing orthogonal to their long axis applies to somatic cells or embryos and is the result of spindle alignment with the longest axis of the cell.
source: The century old observation of cells dividing orthogonal to their long axis applies to somatic cells (Wyatt et al., 2015) or embryos (Minc and Piel, 2012) and is the result of spindle alignment with the longest axis of the cell.
evidence: Supported by citations to Wyatt et al., 2015 and Minc and Piel, 2012

claim: Spindle alignment with the longest axis of the cell is thought to be mediated by cytoplasmic dynein-dependent pulling forces that scale with astral microtubules length.
source: This alignment is thought to be mediated by cytoplasmic dynein-dependent pulling forces that scale with astral microtubules length (Li and Jiang, 2018; Minc and Piel, 2012; Minc et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li and Jiang, 2018; Minc and Piel, 2012; Minc et al., 2011

claim: There are numerous examples where cell shape does not predict spindle orientation in somatic cells.
source: Although cell shape often predicts spindle orientation, there are numerous examples where this is not the case in somatic cells (Finegan and Bergstralh, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Finegan and Bergstralh, 2019

claim: Deviations from the length-dependent spindle positioning mechanism are usually due to local alteration of microtubule-associated forces by polarity domains.
source: These deviations from the length-dependent spindle positioning mechanism are usually due to local alteration of microtubule-associated forces by polarity domains.
evidence: Represents established scientific understanding in the field

claim: Polarity domains can be cortical enrichment of molecular motors such as Dynein.
source: Such polarity domains can be cortical enrichment of molecular motors such as Dynein (Grill et al., 2001; Kotak and Gönczy, 2013), polarity proteins such as Ezrin in epithelial cells (Hebert et al., 2012; Korotkevich et al., 2017), or organelles like yolk granules (Pierre et al., 2016) as well as local actomyosin-driven tension (Scarpa et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grill et al., 2001; Kotak and Gönczy, 2013

claim: Cell geometry and polarity domains are in direct competition to orient the spindle.
source: This has led to the notion that cell geometry and polarity domains are in direct competition to orient the spindle (Niwayama et al., 2019; Pierre et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Niwayama et al., 2019; Pierre et al., 2016

claim: Such competition between cell geometry and polarity domains is thought to occur during early embryonic cleavages to shape whole embryos and to ensure robust cellular patterning in the mouse blastocyst.
source: Such competition is thought to occur during early embryonic cleavages to shape whole embryos (Pierre et al., 2016) and to ensure robust cellular patterning in the mouse blastocyst (Niwayama et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pierre et al., 2016 and Niwayama et al., 2019

claim: UCD divides the mother cell into two daughter cells of different sizes.
source: UCD divides the mother cell into two daughter cells of different sizes.
evidence: Definition of UCD based on established scientific knowledge

claim: UCD shapes early embryogenesis in several animal phyla and sculpts entire organs.
source: This process shapes early embryogenesis in several animal phyla (Hasley et al., 2017; Martín-Durán et al., 2016; McDougall et al., 2019) and sculpts entire organs (Winkley et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hasley et al., 2017; Martín-Durán et al., 2016; McDougall et al., 2019; Winkley et al., 2019

claim: UCDs are often associated with asymmetric segregation of determinants leading to asymmetric cell division creating sibling cells with different cell fates.
source: On top of these morphological outcomes, UCDs are often associated with asymmetric segregation of determinants leading to asymmetric cell division creating sibling cells with different cell fates (Gönczy, 2008; Sardet et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gönczy, 2008; Sardet et al., 2005

claim: One major mechanism to generate UCD relies on spindle off-centering, which can be achieved by local cortical pulling on microtubules or microtubules pushing against the cortex.
source: One major mechanism to generate UCD relies on spindle off-centering, which can be achieved by local cortical pulling on microtubules or microtubules pushing against the cortex.
evidence: Represents established scientific understanding in the field

claim: Cortical anchoring of the microtubule minus-end directed motor Dynein exerts pulling forces able to effectively displace centrosomes and mitotic spindles.
source: Cortical anchoring of the microtubule minus-end directed motor Dynein, by interaction with LGN/Pins/GPR1-2 and/or NuMA/Mud/Lin-5 (di Pietro et al., 2016), exerts pulling forces able to effectively displace centrosomes and mitotic spindles (Grill and Hyman, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to di Pietro et al., 2016 and Grill and Hyman, 2005

claim: Local microtubule pulling forces from the posterior pole of C. elegans zygotes leads to UCD during the first cleavage.
source: Such local microtubule pulling forces from the posterior pole of C. elegans zygotes leads to UCD during the first cleavage (Grill et al., 2001; Kotak and Gönczy, 2013; Redemann et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grill et al., 2001; Kotak and Gönczy, 2013; Redemann et al., 2010

claim: A similar mechanism to cortical pulling is thought to operate also during micromere formation in echinoderm embryos.
source: A similar mechanism is thought to operate also during micromere formation in echinoderm embryos (Poon et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Poon et al., 2019

claim: Cortical pushing can arise when the tip of growing astral microtubule touches the cell cortex creating pushing forces on the spindle.
source: Cortical pushing can arise when the tip of growing astral microtubule touches the cell cortex creating pushing forces on the spindle (Garzon-Coral et al., 2016; Pavin et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Garzon-Coral et al., 2016; Pavin et al., 2012

claim: Asymmetric microtubule cortical pushing caused by asters size asymmetry is thought to be implicated in the UCD of the first cleavage in some spiralian embryos and in ascidian germline precursors.
source: Asymmetric microtubule cortical pushing caused by asters size asymmetry is thought to be implicated in the UCD of the first cleavage in some spiralian embryos (Ren and Weisblat, 2006; Shimizu et al., 1998) and in ascidian germline precursors (Costache et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ren and Weisblat, 2006; Shimizu et al., 1998; Costache et al., 2017

claim: During ascidian notochord development, mother cells with conical shape divide along their center of mass, giving rise to daughter cells with unequal size.
source: For instance, during ascidian notochord development, mother cells with conical shape divide along their center of mass, giving rise to daughter cells with unequal size (Winkley et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Winkley et al., 2019

claim: A rare but extensively studied mechanism of UCD is found in neuroblasts of Drosophila and C. elegans where instead of the spindle the cleavage furrow is off-centered by polarized cortical contractility.
source: Finally, a rare but extensively studied mechanism of UCD is found in neuroblasts of Drosophila and C. elegans where instead of the spindle the cleavage furrow is off-centered by polarized cortical contractility (Cabernard et al., 2010; Kaltschmidt et al., 2000; Ou et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cabernard et al., 2010; Kaltschmidt et al., 2000; Ou et al., 2010

claim: The early embryo of the ascidian Phallusia mammillata has been an emergent model to study mechanisms of UCD due to its invariant cleavage pattern with UCDs in the germline precursors.
source: The early embryo of the ascidian Phallusia mammillata has been an emergent model to study mechanisms of UCD due to its invariant cleavage pattern with UCDs in the germline precursors (Costache et al., 2017; Prodon et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Costache et al., 2017; Prodon et al., 2010

claim: Spindle positioning and cleavage pattern in somatic lineages are predominantly determined by cell shape in ascidian embryos.
source: Whereas spindle positioning and cleavage pattern in somatic lineages are predominantly determined by cell shape, a macromolecular cortical structure, called the centrosome-attracting-body (CAB), overrides the influence of cell shape to off-center the spindle, thereby inducing three successive UCDs from the 8-cell stage (Dumollard et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dumollard et al., 2017

claim: The CAB overrides the influence of cell shape to off-center the spindle, thereby inducing three successive UCDs from the 8-cell stage in ascidian embryos.
source: Whereas spindle positioning and cleavage pattern in somatic lineages are predominantly determined by cell shape, a macromolecular cortical structure, called the centrosome-attracting-body (CAB), overrides the influence of cell shape to off-center the spindle, thereby inducing three successive UCDs from the 8-cell stage (Dumollard et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dumollard et al., 2017

claim: The CAB is inherited by the smaller daughter cells at the posterior pole of the embryo from 16-cell stage onwards.
source: The CAB is inherited by the smaller daughter cells at the posterior pole of the embryo from 16-cell stage onwards, consistent with a decisive role of the CAB in off-centering of the mitotic spindle.
evidence: Represents an observation from the study

claim: Spindle tilting as a mechanism determining UCD dependent of cell shape anisotropies might be largely restricted to early cleavage stages in ascidians.
source: Thus, in ascidians spindle tilting as a mechanism determining UCD dependent of cell shape anisotropies might be largely restricted to early cleavage stages, while at later stages other mechanisms, such as spindle off-centering by polarity domains, might become more important, as found in the germline precursors with spindle off-centering by the CAB (Costache et al., 2017; Prodon et al., 2010).
evidence: Inferred from the study's findings and supported by citations to Costache et al., 2017; Prodon et al., 2010

claim: From the 16-cell stage onwards cells undergo more pronounced mitotic rounding by decreasing their apical cortical tension, which also allows mitotic cells to be deformable by extrinsic forces implementing tension-oriented cell divisions.
source: This effect is restricted to early cleavage stages, as from the 16-cell stage onwards cells undergo more pronounced mitotic rounding by decreasing their apical cortical tension, which also allows mitotic cells to be deformable by extrinsic forces implementing tension-oriented cell divisions (McDougall et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to McDougall et al., 2019

claim: In ascidian embryos, the CAB is thought to attract one spindle pole toward the posterior cortex of the embryo, thereby generating three successive rounds of UCD from the 8-cell stage onwards where the CAB is consistently inherited by the smaller daughter cell.
source: In ascidian embryos, the CAB is thought to attract one spindle pole toward the posterior cortex of the embryo, thereby generating three successive rounds of UCD from the 8-cell stage onwards where the CAB is consistently inherited by the smaller daughter cell, eventually giving rise to two germline precursors at the 64-cell (Negishi et al., 2007; Prodon et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Negishi et al., 2007; Prodon et al., 2010

claim: Cell shape anisotropy at mitosis directs spindle alignment to the vegetal cortex away from the CAB, thereby mitigating the activity of the CAB in pulling the spindle toward the posterior of the cell.
source: Our data resolve this paradox by showing that (1) in addition to the CAB, there is a vegetal polarity domain with no microtubule pulling forces and (2) cell shape anisotropy at mitosis directs spindle alignment to the vegetal cortex away from the CAB, thereby mitigating the activity of the CAB in pulling the spindle toward the posterior of the cell.
evidence: Main conclusion of the study based on experimental data

claim: The forces exerted on microtubules to position the spindle in early ascidian embryo were proposed to originate from cytoplasmic dynein.
source: The forces exerted on microtubules to position the spindle in early ascidian embryo were proposed to originate from cytoplasmic dynein (Pelletier et al., 2020) which has also been proposed to constitute the main mechanism operating in very large cells (Kotak et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pelletier et al., 2020 and Kotak et al., 2013

claim: In smaller cells like in ascidians, the astral microtubules can easily reach the cell cortex, which can then also apply pulling forces on those microtubules.
source: However, in smaller cells like in ascidians, the astral microtubules can easily reach the cell cortex, which can then also apply pulling forces on those microtubules.
evidence: Inferred from the study's observations and general knowledge

claim: A combination of cytoplasmic and cortical microtubule forces is likely involved in precise spindle positioning in early ascidian embryos.
source: Thus, a combination of cytoplasmic and cortical microtubule forces is likely involved in precise spindle positioning in early ascidian embryos.
evidence: Inferred from the study's observations
